Odisha’s Housing & Urban Development Department today held a high-level meeting to deliberate on mitigation strategies and preparedness for urbanheatwavese and flooding, along with modernisation of storm-water drainage systems across major urban areas of the State.
The meeting was chaired by Additional Chief Secretary, Housing & Urban Development Department, Usha Padhee, IAS, at Kharavela Bhawan. SRC Rajesh Pravakar Patil, Municipal Director Arindam Dakua, BMC Commissioner Chanchal Rana, Additional Secretary, H&UD, Rabindra Sahu, EIC, PHEO, Bilas Behera, EIC, OWSSB, Bhagyadhar Mohanty, and other senior officers were present.
The meeting focused on evolving a coordinated and implementation-oriented framework for strengthening urban preparedness and resilience. Detailed discussions were held on preparation of DPRs, funding arrangements, capacity building, technical support and institutional mechanisms for implementation. The focus was on all six Municipal Corporations as well as important major towns in other Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), particularly areas requiring priority interventions.
Addressing the meeting, ACS Padhee emphasised the need to bring all relevant stakeholders on board and develop a clear Action Plan with defined responsibilities and timelines. She suggested that the matter may also be taken up formally at the upcoming Urban Conclave to facilitate wider stakeholder participation and coordinated action.
She stressed the importance of identifying key stakeholders, including the Central Water Commission (CWC) and other concerned agencies, and bringing them together on a common platform. The concerned officers were advised to convene a meeting with the stakeholders and share the identified action points so that all agencies can work in a coordinated manner.
On urban heatwave preparedness, Smt. Padhee called for identification of hotspots requiring immediate intervention in ULBs, along with a set of common interventions that can be undertaken across urban areas. She emphasised the need for clear guidelines indicating the measures that can be taken up immediately and the funding sources that may be utilised for their implementation.
She stressed that the immediate objective should be to ensure that concrete interventions are in place to provide tangible relief to citizens before the next summer. At the same time, she called for systematic planning of medium- and long-term measures to strengthen urban resilience.
The ACS also emphasised the need for long-term interventions such as plantation and other nature-based measures in coordination with the Forest Department. She called for systematic examination of issues relating to plantation, building rules and bye-laws, Schedule of Rates and other relevant regulatory and planning provisions so that necessary interventions can be taken forward in a coordinated manner.
Capacity building was identified as another important component of the proposed strategy. ACS Padhee suggested that the Odisha Urban Academy may be leveraged for structured training programmes for officials and technical personnel. She called for preparation of suitable training modules so that capacity-building activities can be taken up through the Academy.
With regard to storm-water management, ACS Padhee directed the Urban Planning Section to take up the issue on priority. She proposed entering into an MoU for the purpose and suggested that, thereafter, the concerned section of OWSSB may facilitate engagement of a Project Management Consultant (PMC).
She further proposed creation of a dedicated cell or appropriate institutional mechanism for implementing Storm-Water Action Plans. Such a mechanism would also facilitate preparation of DPRs and provide the technical support required for effective implementation of the proposed interventions.
ACS Padhee emphasised that immediate interventions should go hand in hand with medium- and long-term measures. She called for a clear focus on implementation, inter-agency coordination and delivery of tangible outcomes, with the objective of strengthening urban preparedness and resilience and providing visible relief to citizens before the next summer.
The meeting laid emphasis on translating the deliberations into a structured Action Plan covering priority interventions, stakeholder coordination, funding, technical support, capacity building and institutional mechanisms for implementation.
This version positions the meeting as a strategic planning/way-forward meeting, rather than a review of past performance.
Yajati K. Rout is a dynamic journalist at Pragativadi, known for delivering nuanced and impactful storytelling that spans Odisha’s societal fabric to global sports arenas. His reporting navigates seamlessly between grassroots realities, high-profile political developments, and the pulse of international tennis and cricket. With a flair for SEO-driven storytelling and a deep cultural lens, Yajati crafts content that resonates with a diverse readership—bridging insight with accessibility.

South Korean spinach prices rise 51.9% after heatwave
South Korea's grower price index rose 0.2% month-on-month in August 2026, reversing a 0.4% decline in July, according to provisional figures from the Bank of Korea. The index reached 129.64, based on 2020=100, and was 7.9% higher year-on-year.
Agricultural, forestry and fishery product prices increased 3.8% during the month, with the summer heatwave affecting crop supply. Agricultural product prices alone rose 4.9%.
Spinach recorded one of the largest increases, with prices rising 51.9% as high temperatures reduced yields. Pork prices increased 2.8% following livestock mortality and tighter supply.
Energy costs also moved higher. Industrial city gas rates increased 11%, contributing to a 0.9% rise in the power, gas, water and waste management category.
The domestic supply price index declined 1.3% in August as exchange-rate movements and lower international oil prices in July reduced import prices. Intermediate goods prices fell 1.0%, raw materials declined 4.6%, and final goods decreased 0.9%. Total output prices were down 1.2% month-on-month but remained 15.2% above August 2025.
Cost pressure could increase again in September. According to the Bank of Korea, the average Dubai crude oil price as of September 16 was 29% above the previous month's average. The wholesale rate for industrial city gas was also raised by another 6.6% in September.

The developing climate event poses a significant public health threat, with the gravest effects expected in places with droughts.AFP file
Geneva: A rapidly strengthening El Niño could trigger health consequences across the world, worsening malnutrition, cholera, mosquito-borne diseases and heat-related illness as extreme weather places additional pressure on vulnerable communities, United Nations agencies warned on Tuesday.
The World Health Organization warned that the developing climate event poses a significant public health threat, with the gravest effects expected in places where droughts, floods and extreme heat collide with fragile health systems, limited access to care, food insecurity, displacement and humanitarian emergencies.
Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here.
“The most severe impacts will be experienced” where those pressures overlap, Teresa Zakaria, head of the WHO unit for risk reduction, humanitarian operations and climate change, told reporters in Geneva.
Zakaria called El Niño “a significant public health threat, not just a climate phenomenon”, warning that its effects could extend well beyond changes in temperature and rainfall.
Among the most immediate concerns are malnutrition and cholera, which the WHO assesses as very high risks in areas affected by both drought and flooding.
Climate shocks can damage crops and livelihoods, reduce access to safe water and sanitation and place already stretched health services under further strain.
More than 150 million people are already experiencing acute food insecurity worldwide, according to Zakaria, with the number expected to rise as disrupted rainfall and extreme weather affect food production and household incomes.
Changing temperatures and rainfall patterns could also create more favourable conditions for mosquito-borne diseases. The WHO has warned of increased risks from malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika, including the possibility that some diseases could spread into areas where they have not traditionally circulated.
Heavy rainfall and flooding can create breeding grounds for disease-carrying mosquitoes, while floods may contaminate water supplies and increase the risk of cholera. Drought, meanwhile, can deepen food shortages, worsen malnutrition and make access to clean water more difficult.
Extreme heat presents another concern, particularly for people with existing health conditions and those with limited access to cooling or medical care.
Armel Castellan, an extreme heat adviser with the joint WHO-WMO Climate and Health Programme, noted that the world had just experienced two record-hot months, while sea-surface temperatures were also at unprecedented levels.
As El Niño approaches its expected peak towards the end of 2026, much of the Southern Hemisphere, including southern Africa, South America and Australia, will be moving into its hottest season in early 2027. That combination could heighten the risks of drought, wildfires, smoke and deteriorating air quality, Castellan explained.
The World Meteorological Organization earlier this month forecast that El Niño would intensify into a very strong event before peaking towards the end of the year. Its latest modelling shows a nearly 100 per cent likelihood that El Niño will persist through February 2027, with its effects on rainfall and temperature continuing well into next year.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern associated with unusually warm ocean conditions in the tropical Pacific. It can reshape rainfall and temperature patterns around the world, increasing the likelihood of drought in some regions and heavy rain or flooding in others. The strength of an El Niño event, however, does not translate directly into the same level of impact everywhere.
The current episode is unfolding against a backdrop of exceptionally high global temperatures, amplifying concern over its potential consequences.
“Every El Niño is different,” Castellan told reporters. But this episode is interacting with temperatures that were already breaking records, creating what he described as an unusual combination of climate risks.
The WHO is urging governments to use the months before the event reaches its peak to strengthen health-system preparedness, improve disease surveillance, protect continuity of medical care and ensure that medicines and other supplies are available in areas most exposed to climate shocks.
Zakaria urged governments, communities and humanitarian partners to act before those risks intensify.
“We have a window of opportunity to act now before these risks become crises,” she stressed.

articles.title: Mapping student life in a heatwave - Varsity Online

Autumn has arrived. As temperatures drop and the evenings draw in, we prepare for the start of a new academic year. Cambridge will be a perfect postcard of dark academia, complete with falling leaves, misty mornings and college puffer jackets. But September also comes as a huge sigh of relief after the UK’s hottest summer on record. And as headlines continue to promise, 2026 might just have been “the coolest summer for the rest of our lives”.
The record-breaking heatwaves of May and June caused universal discomfort, distraction and disruption at the University during its busiest months of the year.
We surveyed dozens of students to reflect on the everyday experiences of extreme heat in Cambridge, and mapped the specific challenges for the University in the face of climate change. Conversations with local experts revealed the wider discussion and potential solutions to “unwanted heat”.
Student experiences
On entering my own room in Easter term, I would collapse, disrobe and run a cold shower, desperate to cool off and wash away the sweat. That kind of sweat that covers the body, makes your clothes and hair stick to your skin, and leaves you feeling disgusting. One student surveyed said they could “physically feel the intensity” of the heat entering their accommodation stairwell. For another, even a short walk would leave them sweaty, meaning “you don’t even want to go outside”. As a result, the typical image of a Cambridge student was abandoned, as travelling by bike became something to avoid at all costs.
“Other people have the same ideas, so cool rooms end up being hotter anyway, because they are more crowded”
Cambridge is a vibrant mix of colleges, libraries, lectures, cafés, green spaces and more. As much as we like to talk about how far, far away Girton is, compared to most other university cities, Cambridge is incredibly easy to get around. Yet the heat made travel undesirable and our worlds shrank to be even smaller. Many students remained in what few cool spaces existed in college, but as Sheng, a second-year student explained, this approach was not infallible. “Other people have the same ideas, so cool rooms end up being hotter anyway, because [they are] more crowded.”
Easter term for most is characterised by locking oneself in the library; however, this summer saw many libraries become almost uninhabitable. Students in our survey described college and faculty libraries as “unbearable,” “unusable,” and “quite awful,” with almost every respondent mentioning the heat, crowding and lack of fans or air conditioning as a major factor impacting their study routines. The UL’s main reading room and the Haddon Library both closed when the heat was at its most extreme.
Air-conditioned rooms became hot property, and in a far cry from the “aesthetic” study spots typically associated with Oxbridge, one student reported working out of McDonald’s. West Hub, a vague group of “niche” and “obscure” spots, and public cafés were also popular – though the latter came with a price, and did not promise the quiet desk, power outlets or strong WiFi of purpose-built study spaces. Some students also pointed to the added heat of studying with your laptop on your lap, along with the unfortunate need to blur lines between “relaxing and working areas” to stay cool.
For those who braved the libraries, the heat left people uncomfortable, tired, and “struggling to concentrate”. In a recent Science article for Varsity, Reuben Tao looked at how heat impacts your brain and ability to study: heat literally detracts from our “cognitive ‘bandwidth’,” as well as impacting sleep, which is an incredibly important part of memory processes.
Many student respondents reported poor sleep and fatigue in Easter term, and described their improvised attempts to cool their rooms. One Caius student wrote about people moving their mattresses outside, and most students relied on fans; one individual “had to buy several fans, because my window only opened about 10cm,” while another “wanted to buy a fan, but they all got expensive or out of stock”. Universally, curtains were shut during the day and windows opened at night. Students battened down the hatches and rode out the heatwave.
But what does all this disruption and adaptation amount to? Science can explain the impact of heat on the mind and body, but it is our routines that reveal the importance of behaviour and infrastructure: where individuals can adapt, and where institutions should provide support. Indeed, behavioral adaptation can place an unfair financial burden on individuals and is not possible for all. One student, for example, felt unsafe at night leaving the window open, and others had medication interfere with their body’s natural heat regulation, making it harder to cope with the same conditions.
Professor Mike Hulme of the University’s Geography department points to the much-forgotten psychological perception of the climate as another important factor.
What counts as a heatwave?
“If we just focus on meteorology, we’ve got a whole variety of different definitions of when a heatwave is triggered,” Professor Hulme tells us. He points to how the official definition of a heatwave differs around the globe, and even across the UK – in Scotland, the temperature only needs to reach 25°C for three consecutive days, “which just passes without any commentary at all”. In Cambridge, three consecutive days reaching or exceeding 30°C are classified as a heatwave.
“You Brits have NO IDEA”
Beyond location, individuals experience heat differently. The “physiological experience of heat […] varies by age. It varies by gender. It varies by ethnicity, and where your earlier years, your formative years [were spent], so the whole idea of acclimatisation”.
“You Brits have NO IDEA,” one international student respondent wrote. “The heatwave in France felt like the sun was personally crushing me. The heat is noticeably milder here, your nights are cool, my parents kept telling me it was super-hot for the whole of July, you know we had megafires also.”
It is also important to remind ourselves that climate change is a more acute crisis for the global majority – both in exposure to risk and capacity to adapt. In the UK, climate change is making our homes hotter. It is not (yet) sinking our homes into the sea.
In fact, the relatively mild climate of the UK means that hot summers are often desired. Many Brits “want their summers to be full of sunshine and to be warm, […] so you can be out at 11 o’clock at night, down by the river, having drinks,” Hulme said. He draws a crucial distinction between wanted and unwanted heat, and mentions the disproportionate effects of high temperatures on vulnerable people. “Who is it unwanted for, and why is it unwanted? And if it is unwanted, what do you do about it?”
Dealing with “unwanted heat” in Cambridge
For Cambridge students in Easter term, high temperatures might not be a health risk, but the heat is most definitely unwanted, and the University’s numerous centuries-old can make finding solutions uniquely complex.
Where wealthy nations like the UK can afford to adapt their infrastructure, architecture is often the first topic of discussion. International students all raised the poor design of British buildings for withstanding heat and remarked that our empirically cooler summers felt “less tolerable” than hot weather in countries like China and Lebanon. This is especially true of very old buildings; as one student put it, “college buildings have an amazing ability to freeze you in winter and boil you in summer.”
We received mixed perspectives on accommodation in the heat. Factors like the direction windows faced, age, and flooring material created differences in temperature, while price did not seem to play a role. Despite the lack of air conditioning being a common complaint, and air-conditioned study spaces becoming a ‘holy grail’ in Easter term, almost all respondents felt that installing University-wide air conditioning would be impractical and environmentally irresponsible. Most students felt there was a balance to be struck. “Some of the largest libraries ought to be [air-conditioned], and only utilised when necessary, otherwise it’s just contributing to the issue,” one student wrote.
“Almost all respondents felt that installing University-wide air conditioning would be impractical and environmentally irresponsible”
Professor Ronita Bardhan, an Architecture professor and head of the Cambridge Sustainable Design Group, is acutely aware of the challenges and opportunities, of climate-, student- and health-conscious updates to the University. “Given Cambridge’s heterogeneous estate, we need what I call in my research ‘precision retrofit’,” combining “multi-disciplinary knowledge of building physics, environmental design” and observation technology “to identify where heat is lost in colder months, where overheating occurs in summer, and where interventions will deliver greatest benefit.”
“Climate-conscious design does not have to mean replacing buildings or radically altering their architecture.” Still, the University already offers several “compelling examples” of innovative climate design, such as Selwyn’s Bartlam Library, Magdalene’s New Library, and student accommodation at Lucy Cavendish and King’s Cranmer Road, which “demonstrate Passivhaus and low-carbon approaches”.
However, Professor Bardhan points out that “there is no silver bullet for all buildings in Cambridge.” In many cases, as with the rest of the UK, structural intervention is impossible or irresponsible. As well as historic buildings, the city’s climate experiences relatively little extreme weather.
Professor Hulme seconds this. Retro-fitting would come “at a huge cost to society at large for a relatively small number of days. This is not Sweden, and this is not Singapore.” It is our responsibility to “get this balance right between behavioral adaptations and infrastructural changes”.
“People need to take responsibility for their weather.”
As students, unlike bus drivers petitioning for “heat breaks” during shifts in vehicle cabs that can reach up to 50°C, we are privileged to have a lot of agency over when, where and how we study, especially in Easter term. Professor Hulme speaks about restructuring his own work days to “be up at 6 o’clock in the morning and get most of my serious work done by midday,” followed by a “Mediterranean style siesta” to avoid the hottest hours. Indeed, “people live all over the world in all sorts of very extreme climates and extreme weathers, and they do so by adapting, by acclimatising, and they do that primarily by behaviour.”
“People need to take responsibility for their weather”
Several international students brought up behavioural adaptation in their survey answers. One respondent from Hong Kong remarked that “in the UK, people don’t really have good cooling strategies,” while another specified that people in China do not go “outside during midday/the peak of the heat,” and use “minifans or umbrellas when we’re in the sun”.
Prof. Hulme acknowledges that individual circumstances vary, and some have more freedom than others to change their lifestyles during a heatwave. University-wide strategies must be combined with personal action, with our community taking responsibility “within whatever constraints we find ourselves”.
In a statement to Varsity, a spokesperson for Cambridge Climate Society echoed the importance of balance as we look to the future. “Simple actions like maintaining ventilation and closing curtains during daytime can help us adapt, alongside creating greener, more climate-resilient living. […] This experience of extreme heat serves as an alarming reminder of the realities of a changing climate and the need to situate it within broader discussions of university life, infrastructure and wellbeing.”
Support Varsity
Varsity is the independent newspaper for the University of Cambridge, established in its current form in 1947. In order to maintain our editorial independence, our print newspaper and news website receives no funding from the University of Cambridge or its constituent Colleges.
We are therefore almost entirely reliant on advertising for funding and we expect to have a tough few months and years ahead.
In spite of this situation, we are going to look at inventive ways to look at serving our readership with digital content and of course in print too!
Therefore we are asking our readers, if they wish, to make a donation from as little as £1, to help with our running costs. Many thanks, we hope you can help!

Heavy rains lash Hyderabad, IMD issues red alert in 8 districts
IMD Hyderabad forecast very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall, potentially exceeding 204.5 mm of rainfall, between Wednesday, September 23, and Friday, September 25.
Hyderabad: Heavy rains lashed parts of Hyderabad on Tuesday, September 22, prompting the Chief Minister to put the administration on alert. Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Hyderabad, issued a red alert for eight districts in Telangana from Wednesday.
Telangana weather enthusiast T Balaji took to X to warn of intense rainfall across various parts of Hyderabad on Tuesday evening.
He said, “Areas including Alwal, Balanagar, Qutbullapur, Gajularamaram, Malkajgiri, Kapra, Bowenpally, SEC-BAD, Himayatnagar, Khairthabad, Musheerabad, OU, Amberpet, Uppal, Nagole, LB Nagar, Malakpet, Tank Bund, Vanasthalipuram, Hayathnagar, Charminar and nearby areas during 5.30 pm and 7 pm.”
He also said that other areas in the city would experience isolated thunderstorms.
CM’s instructions for official machinery
The Chief Minister instructed the Commissioners of the three Municipal Corporations in the greater Hyderabad region, HYDRAA, and police commissioners to work in coordination and monitor the situation.
The civic authorities have been asked to take immediate measures to prevent waterlogging on main roads, junctions, and residential colonies.
The CM also instructed the Energy Department to ensure there are no power outages. The Traffic Police wing has also been directed to take proactive measures to prevent traffic congestion.
Red alert in other districts
The IMD, Hyderabad, has issued a red alert for multiple districts in Telangana. It has forecast very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall, potentially exceeding 204.5 mm, between Wednesday, September 23, and Friday, September 25.
The red alert specifically covers the districts of Peddapalli, Jayashankar Bhupalapally, Mulugu, Bhadradri Kothagudem, Khammam, Mahabubabad, Warangal, and Hanamkonda.
In addition to the warning, the IMD has issued an orange alert indicating heavy to very heavy rainfall (ranging between 64.4 mm and 204.5 mm) for isolated places in Kumaram Bheem Asifabad, Mancherial, Jagtial, Rajanna Sircilla, Karimnagar, Nalgonda, Suryapet, Jangaon and Siddipet districts.
